results.summary: This project implements the 74HC595 shift register, which takes serial data and outputs it in parallel. It is designed to drive up to 8 LEDs, and the author successfully tested it with a Knight Rider effect using a Pmod LED module and custom C/MicroPython code. The design requires external LEDs or a similar output device to be observed. It is a common component for expanding microcontroller output capabilities.

This design is a High-Level Synthesis (HLS) implementation of the Monobit test from the NIST 800.22 standard, used for evaluating random number generators. It processes one bit per clock cycle and outputs a randomness validation signal every 65536 cycles. The design requires a clock input and a bit stream as input, with no external hardware currently needed. The output is valid only when a specific signal is high.

This project plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and requires a 3125 Hz clock and a reset signal. The audio output is generated across two pins, and a piezo speaker must be connected externally. The design demonstrates a creative use of digital outputs for audio generation.

This project converts binary input into signals suitable for driving a 7-segment display to show hexadecimal characters. The specific functionality, testing procedures, and required external hardware are not detailed in the provided documentation. It is noted to be implemented using Wokwi, suggesting a focus on simulation and educational purposes. Further documentation is needed to fully understand its operation and use.

This project features the LaRVa RISC-V CPU with a serial port and JTAG interface for debugging. It requires external SRAM memory and address latches, which connect to the PMOD ports. A bootloader is included to load programs via the serial port, and basic testing involves sending an 'L' character over serial. The design is intended for embedded applications requiring a small RISC-V core with external memory.

This project implements a 4-bit successive approximation Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) operating at 5 MHz. It requires an external sample-and-hold circuit to maintain a constant analog input voltage during conversion. The ADC takes an analog input and a clock, with an active-low reset signal that should be pulsed after each conversion cycle. The digital output represents the converted analog value, and the conversion completes in 5 clock cycles.

This is a simple, single-stage RISC-V CPU designed based on university lecture material. Instructions are 32-bit but are loaded over an 8-bit input bus across four clock cycles. The CPU outputs the ALU result, and has pins for reset and instruction memory write enable. Verification was performed using testbench simulations, and no external hardware is required for its basic operation. The design focuses on educational purposes for understanding RISC-V architecture.

This module serves as a factory test for TinyTapeout 05, providing two modes of operation controlled by an input pin. When the control pin is high, a counter is output on all output pins; otherwise, the input pins are mirrored to the output pins. Testing involves setting the control pin high and observing the toggling outputs. This design allows for basic verification of the chip's output capabilities.

This project implements an 8-bit Concurrent Built-In Logic Block Observer (CBILBO) designed for memory testing. It utilizes shift registers, logic gates, flip-flops, and multiplexers to provide internal feedback and observation capabilities. The design supports asynchronous reset and clocked logic, with dedicated input and output paths for integration into the Tiny Tapeout shuttle. Testing involves simulating stimulus and verifying the shifting and feedback behavior of the register stages. No external hardware is required.

This project displays selectable Latin characters on a 7-segment display, implemented using Wokwi. Six input DIP switches are used to select the character, with inputs 7 and 8 left unconnected. The display is driven segment by segment, requiring a sufficiently high clock rate (1000 Hz is suggested) to be visible. The design includes a mapping for numbers, letters, and some punctuation, intended for educational purposes. Successful testing involves selecting characters and observing them on the display.
